title: LINC: Decoupling Local Consequence Scoring from Hidden Matching in Constructive Neural Routing
claim: Even very capable models can fail at a simple exact one-step comparison, motivating explicit computation of such quantities externally.
layout: Single panel, top-to-bottom dialogue, cartoon avatars with speech bubbles
description: A single cartoon dialogue in anime chibi style. At top left, a circular avatar of a brown-haired boy with a hand on his chin and a blue question mark asks in a white speech bubble, "Is 9.8 larger than 9.11?". At bottom right, a blue-haired maid-like character with floppy ears and a bored, unimpressed expression answers in a light-blue speech bubble, "9.11 is larger.", which is wrong. Sparkle icons surround the responder. The palette is mostly blue, navy outlines and white background. The eye goes first to the large question bubble, then to the incorrect answer and the character below. The figure illustrates a simple failure case with no technical diagrams or math notation.
caption: Even very large language models can fail at a one-step exact comparison; such computations are usually delegated to an external program.
abstract: Constructive neural routing solvers usually score the next action by matching a decoder context against candidate embeddings computed once per instance from static node features such as coordinates, demands, and time windows; deterministic one-step consequences such as travel, waiting, slack, and capacity changes are not provided as inputs and must be inferred implicitly by the model. We propose LINC, a decoder-side candidate decision architecture that decouples computing these consequences from learning how much they matter. The environment computes the consequences explicitly at each step; candidate-level consequences are scored by a state-conditioned shared linear comparator, while feasible-set summaries modulate the decoder context. This keeps the cached embeddings and standard global matching while giving the scoring function direct access to deterministic transition quantities. The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW) serves as the main constrained-routing testbed, and the same interface extends to the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) and Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). Across external benchmarks and no-retraining scale-transfer settings, LINC consistently improves strong neural baselines, with the advantage becoming more pronounced as test size moves further beyond the training scale, especially on constrained routing problems.
